mainEntity.name: How much wax do I need for a candle?

acceptedAnswer.text: Multiply your container volume by the wax density for your type. For soy wax, one pound fills about 20 oz of container volume. A typical 8 oz candle needs roughly 6.4 oz (0.4 lb) of soy wax.
Fragrance load is the percentage of fragrance oil relative to the total wax weight. Most waxes support 6-10% fragrance load. Soy wax typically maxes at 10-12%, while paraffin can hold 6-10%.

mainEntity.name: What is the density of soy wax?

acceptedAnswer.text: Soy wax has a density of approximately 0.9 g/ml (or about 0.86 oz per fluid oz of volume). This means soy wax shrinks slightly when cooling, so containers may need a second pour.

mainEntity.name: How much dye do I use per pound of wax?

acceptedAnswer.text: Liquid dye typically uses 3-10 drops per pound of wax, while dye blocks use about 0.1-0.2 oz per pound. Start small and increase until you reach your desired color intensity.

mainEntity.name: Should I fill my candle container all the way?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Fill containers to about 85-90% capacity to leave room for the wick and prevent overflow. This calculator accounts for this fill percentage automatically.

mainEntity.name: What's the difference between soy and paraffin wax?

acceptedAnswer.text: Soy wax is natural, burns cleaner, and has a lower melting point. Paraffin is petroleum-based, holds more fragrance, and produces brighter colors. Soy is denser so you need less by volume but more by weight.

howItWorks:
How the Candle Wax Calculator Works

This calculator turns your container's fluid-ounce or milliliter volume into the number that matters at the pour pot: a wax weight, plus the fragrance oil and dye that scale off of it. It doesn't treat wax as interchangeable — soy, paraffin, beeswax, and coconut blends each have a different density, so the same jar yields a different wax weight depending which one you select.

Wax Weight = Container Volume × Fill % × Wax Density
  • Fill percentage (typically 85-90%) leaves room for the wick and prevents overflow
  • Wax density varies by type — soy is lighter than paraffin or beeswax
  • Fragrance oil is calculated as a percentage of the wax weight (6-10% typical)
  • Dye amount is estimated at ~0.1 oz per pound of wax for medium color

Example: A 9 oz tin with paraffin wax at 90% fill = 9 × 0.90 × 0.90 ≈ 7.29 oz of wax per candle — about 207 g at paraffin's ≈0.90 g/mL density. At an 8% fragrance load, that adds roughly 16.5 g of fragrance oil, best poured around 160-180°F once the wax and fragrance are fully blended.
faqHTML:
Frequently Asked Questions

How much wax do I need for a candle?

The amount depends on your container volume and wax type. Multiply the container volume by the fill percentage (85%) and the wax density. For soy wax, an 8 oz container needs about 5.8 oz of wax.

What is fragrance load percentage?

Fragrance load is the percentage of fragrance oil relative to wax weight. Most waxes support 6-10%. Going above the recommended maximum can cause sweating, poor burn, or safety issues.

What is the density of soy wax?

Soy wax has a density of approximately 0.86 oz per fluid ounce (0.90 g/ml). It is lighter than paraffin (0.90 oz/fl oz) and beeswax (0.96 oz/fl oz).

How much dye do I use per pound of wax?

For liquid dye, use 3-10 drops per pound. For dye blocks, approximately 0.1-0.2 oz per pound. Start light and increase for deeper colors.

Should I fill my candle container all the way?

No. Fill to 85-90% capacity to leave room for the wick, prevent overflow when the wax melts, and allow for a clean finish. This calculator accounts for fill percentage.

What's the difference between soy and paraffin wax?

Soy wax is plant-based, burns cleaner with less soot, and has a lower melting point. Paraffin is petroleum-based, provides better scent throw, and produces more vibrant colors. Coconut blends offer a middle ground.

howWeCalculate.intro: The math here is a short chain, not a black box: container volume sets the ceiling, fill percentage brings it down to a realistic pour target, wax density converts that volume into a weight, and fragrance load and dye ratios scale off that wax weight. Change the wax type and every downstream number moves, because soy, paraffin, beeswax, and coconut blends don't share a density.
steps: Container volume × fill percentage gives the melted-wax volume you're actually pouring, leaving headroom for the wick and preventing overflow at the rim
That volume converts to a weight using your selected wax's density — soy ≈0.9 g/mL, paraffin ≈0.90-0.93 g/mL, beeswax ≈0.96 g/mL, coconut blends ≈0.82-0.85 g/mL
Fragrance oil is calculated as your chosen percentage of that wax weight and reported separately, since it's stirred in after the wax has melted
Dye is estimated from a standard ratio of roughly 0.1-0.2 oz of dye block per pound of wax, scaled to your batch size, as a starting point for color testing
All figures are multiplied by your number of candles so you know exact totals to weigh out before a batch pour
howWeCalculate.disclaimer: These figures are planning estimates, not a substitute for testing. Wax densities vary between manufacturers and even between production batches, and fragrance oils affect set time and hot throw differently depending on the blend. Always do a small test pour and a full burn test — including checking your wick size — before committing to a full batch, and follow your wax and fragrance suppliers' documented maximum-load and safety guidance.

whenToUse.intro: This calculator earns its keep whenever you're planning a pour rather than winging one — sizing a batch, budgeting wax and fragrance oil purchases, or adapting a recipe to a container or wax type you haven't used before.
scenarios: Sizing a wholesale or market batch, where the number-of-candles field multiplies your per-unit wax, fragrance, and dye needs across the whole run
Switching wax types — say from paraffin to soy — where reusing an old recipe's weights would over- or under-fill the container, since the densities differ
Testing a new container or vessel before committing a full case of wax to it, so you know your yield and approximate cost per candle first
Dialing in fragrance load within a wax's supported range (commonly 6-10% for soy and paraffin, up to 10-12% for some soy blends) without guessing at drops
Costing out a recipe for pricing, where knowing exact wax, fragrance oil, and dye weights per candle feeds directly into a per-unit cost calculation

sections.title: What This Calculator Actually Does
sections.body: Candle making runs on two numbers that don't behave the way beginners expect: the volume printed on your jar and the weight of wax that actually goes into it. This calculator bridges that gap. Enter your container's volume in fluid ounces or milliliters, tell it how many candles you're pouring, pick a wax type — soy, paraffin, beeswax, or a coconut blend — and set your fragrance load and fill percentage. It returns four numbers: wax weight per candle, total wax for the batch, fragrance oil to add, and a dye estimate. The reason this needs more than a rule of thumb is density. A fluid ounce of water weighs roughly an ounce, but wax doesn't. Soy wax runs about 0.9 g/mL (≈0.86 oz per fl oz of volume), paraffin sits close behind at 0.90-0.93 g/mL, beeswax is denser at ≈0.96 g/mL, and coconut wax blends run lighter, often 0.82-0.85 g/mL depending on the coconut-to-soy or coconut-to-paraffin ratio the manufacturer uses. Pour the same 8 oz jar with soy and with beeswax and you'll use meaningfully different weights of wax, even though the container is identical.

sections.title: Why Container Volume Isn't the Same as Wax Weight
sections.body: Container volume also isn't the target fill amount. Fill a jar to the brim with melted wax and there's nowhere for the wick, tab, and any wick bar to sit, and you risk wax creeping over the rim as it settles. Most chandlers fill to 85-90% of stated container volume, which is why this calculator treats fill percentage as its own input rather than assuming 100%. There's a second wrinkle specific to natural waxes: soy and coconut blends shrink as they cool and crystallize, which is why many soy candles get a second, smaller repour once the surface has set, to fill in the crater that forms around the wick. Paraffin shrinks too but is more forgiving and less prone to visible sinkholes. Fragrance oil adds a further complication — it isn't wax, so once you add it the total liquid volume and weight both increase, which is why the calculator reports it as an addition on top of the wax weight rather than folding it silently into the total. Worked example: an 8 fl oz jar (≈237 mL) filled to 90% for wick clearance needs about 213 mL of melted wax. At soy wax's typical density of ≈0.9 g/mL, that's roughly 192 g of finished pour weight. At a 6% fragrance load, that splits into about 11.5 g of fragrance oil stirred into about 181 g of wax.

sections.title: When You'll Reach for This Tool
sections.body: Use it any time you're scaling a recipe rather than eyeballing it. It's built for batch planning — set the number of candles to 12 and it multiplies the per-candle wax, fragrance, and dye figures across the whole run, the fastest way to know how many pounds of wax and how many ounces of fragrance oil to order before you start melting. It's equally useful when you switch wax suppliers or wax types mid-project: a recipe tuned for paraffin will under-fill or over-fill a jar if you swap in soy or a coconut blend without recalculating, because the densities aren't interchangeable. Testing a new container is another common case — measure its volume once, run it through the calculator at your usual fragrance load and fill percentage, and you'll know your per-candle yield and rough wax cost before committing a whole batch of wax to an untested vessel.

howToSteps.title: Measure Your Container
howToSteps.description: Find your container's usable volume in fl oz or mL — check the manufacturer spec sheet, or fill it with water and measure, since printed jar sizes are often rounded.

howToSteps.title: Set Wax Type, Batch Size, and Ratios
howToSteps.description: Choose soy, paraffin, beeswax, or coconut blend, enter how many candles you're pouring, and set your fragrance load percentage and fill percentage (85-90% is standard to leave wick clearance).

howToSteps.title: Click Calculate
howToSteps.description: The calculator converts your container volume to a wax weight using that wax type's density, then derives fragrance oil and dye amounts from it.

howToSteps.title: Read Off Wax, Fragrance, and Dye Weights
howToSteps.description: Use the wax-per-candle and total-wax figures to weigh out your pour, the fragrance oil figure to measure your scent addition, and the dye estimate as a starting point — adjust dye to taste on a test pour.

tips: Weigh your container empty, fill it with water, and weigh again to get a true volume in grams (1 g of water ≈ 1 mL) if you don't trust the manufacturer's stated fl oz — printed container volumes are often rounded.

For soy wax, plan on a second, smaller repour once the first pour has set and a sinkhole forms around the wick — this is normal shrinkage, not a failed batch, and the total wax figure should cover both pours combined.

Pour temperature affects finish as much as the recipe does: soy typically pours best around 120-135°F, paraffin container wax around 160-180°F, and beeswax needs to stay hot longer given its ≈144-149°F melting point — check your specific wax's data sheet rather than using one temperature for every type.

Stay inside your wax's tested fragrance load ceiling even if the jar has volume to spare — pushing past it (often 10-12% for soy, 6-10% for paraffin) risks fragrance oil separating out, or 'sweating,' on the surface of the finished candle.
Add fragrance oil and dye after removing wax from heat, not while it's still at pour temperature — many fragrance oils lose scent compounds when held at sustained high heat.

faq.question: Why does the calculator ask for wax type instead of just using container volume?
faq.answer: Because wax types don't share a density. Soy wax is about 0.9 g/mL, paraffin is comparable at 0.90-0.93 g/mL, beeswax is denser at roughly 0.96 g/mL, and coconut blends run lighter at 0.82-0.85 g/mL depending on the blend. The same 8 oz jar takes meaningfully different weights of wax depending which one you pour, which is why the wax weight output changes when you switch the wax type dropdown.

faq.question: Why is my wax weight lower than my container's fluid ounce size?
faq.answer: Two reasons stack together: fill percentage and density. A fill percentage below 100% (85-90% is typical) reserves room for the wick, and most waxes weigh slightly less per fluid ounce than water does. An 8 fl oz jar at 90% fill with soy wax's ≈0.86 oz-per-fl-oz density works out to roughly 8 × 0.90 × 0.86 ≈ 6.2 oz of wax, not 8 oz.

faq.question: How is fragrance oil calculated?
faq.answer: Fragrance oil is calculated as a percentage of your wax weight — the fragrance load you set — and reported as a separate addition. At an 8% load on 180 g of wax, that's roughly 14.4 g of fragrance oil stirred into the melted wax before pouring, on top of the wax weight, not carved out of it.

faq.question: Why does the total change so much when I switch from paraffin to soy?
faq.answer: Mainly density and fragrance ceiling together. Soy is slightly less dense than paraffin by volume, so the raw wax weight moves a little, but the bigger shift is usually that soy tolerates a higher fragrance load (commonly up to 10-12%) than paraffin (commonly 6-10%), so if you're maximizing scent throw the fragrance oil total can shift more than the wax weight does.

faq.question: Do I need to account for a second pour when using this calculator?
faq.answer: The total wax figure covers the full amount of wax that ends up in the candle, including a repour. For soy and coconut blends, which shrink and crater around the wick as they cool, plan to hold back roughly 10% of your melted wax for that second pour rather than pouring the entire batch amount in one go.

faq.question: What if my container has an unusual shape, like a hexagon or tapered tin?
faq.answer: Volume is volume regardless of shape — measure it by filling the container with water and pouring that water into a measuring cup, or weighing it, since 1 mL of water ≈ 1 g, then enter that figure. The wax weight calculation doesn't care whether the container is a straight-sided jar or a tapered tin, only its usable volume.
